claim.pdf_says: D.19.9.3  Files in factory objects (fourth-level subclause of D.19.9 Files in object orientation, whose siblings D.19.9.1 General and D.19.9.2 Files in instance objects are transcribed as '### ')
claim.why_it_matters: D.19.9.3 is emitted one level shallower than its own siblings D.19.9.1 and D.19.9.2 (both '###') and at the same level as its parent '## D.19.9 Files in object orientation', so the markdown outline detaches it from D.19.9 and makes it a peer clause. Same systemic flattening artifact described for page 1150.

verdict.reasoning: REFUTED. The heading is not missing and no text differs. PDF page 1154 prints 'D.19.9.3 Files in factory objects'; specs/ISO_COBOL.md line 46527 carries '## D.19.9.3 Files in factory objects', preceded by the anchor ''. Number, title and word order match verbatim; the only delta is the count of '#' characters, i.e. pure markdown formatting. The claim's kind label 'missing-heading' is therefore factually wrong -- nothing is absent. The claim's load-bearing premise is that the PDF marks D.19.9.3 as a level deeper than D.19.9. It does not. Font metrics extracted with PyMuPDF show all four headings in this family rendered IDENTICALLY: D.19.9 (p1153, Cambria,Bold 11.67pt, y0=343.1), D.19.9.1 (p1153, Cambria,Bold 11.67pt, y0=368.4), D.19.9.2 (p1153, Cambria,Bold 11.67pt, y0=469.6), D.19.9.3 (p1154, Cambria,Bold 11.67pt, y0=568.8). Same face, same size, same weight, same flush-left text margin (x0=80.0 on the recto p1153, x0=63.5 on the verso p1154 -- a mirrored-margin difference, not an indent difference; the running header on each page starts at the same respective x0). For contrast, the true body-level run-in bold on the same page ('Inherited Factory Object Definitions') is 10.70pt. So the PDF encodes ZERO typographic level signal separating D.19.9 from D.19.9.1/.2/.3, and the transcription cannot have dropped a distinction the source never made. The only hierarchy indicator the PDF supplies is the clause number itself, and 'D.19.9.3' is preserved intact inside the heading text -- the parent/child relationship is fully recoverable and no meaning is lost. The 'anomaly' framing also fails. Heading depth shallower than clause numbering is the transcription's document-wide norm, not a page-1154 defect: of 2419 numbered headings in specs/ISO_COBOL.md, 1594 (65.9%) use fewer '#' than their numbering depth -- e.g. '## 4.2.5', '## 5.2.3', and within this very annex '## D.19.3', '## D.19.3.3', '## D.19.4.2', '## D.19.5.2', '## D.19.5.4.2', '## D.19.11.1'. Even the alleged clean siblings sit at '###' while their own numbering depth is 4, so they are flattened too; D.19.9.3 is flattened by one step more. Accepting this finding would oblige the ledger to carry ~1,594 identical entries, none of which change a rule, a general format, a syntax diagram or any normative text. Per the rejection criteria this is formatting that does not change meaning. Verified independently against the rendered page, the PDF font metrics, and the canonical markdown.
verdict.corrected_description: Not a PDF-vs-markdown content discrepancy. The heading is present and verbatim correct ('D.19.9.3 Files in factory objects', with its section anchor). What is true, and all that is true: the markdown emits it as '##' while its siblings D.19.9.1/.2 are '###', so the outline nesting is internally inconsistent. That is a cosmetic normalization item, not a transcription fidelity defect -- the PDF renders D.19.9, D.19.9.1, D.19.9.2 and D.19.9.3 in identical 11.67pt Cambria Bold at the same margin, supplying no level cue to lose, and the hierarchy remains explicit in the retained clause number. If the project ever wants a machine-clean outline, it should be handled as one document-wide pass deriving heading depth from clause numbering (1594 of 2419 numbered headings are affected), not as a per-page structural finding.
